title: The Birth of Jesus and the Boy in the Temple

verses.text: Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire.
This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria.
And everyone went to his own town to register.
So Joseph also went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David called Bethlehem, since he was from the house and line of David.
He went there to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child.
While they were there, the time came for her Child to be born.
And she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.
And there were shepherds residing in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks by night.
Just then an angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified.
But the angel said to them, "Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people:
Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!
And this will be a sign to you: You will find a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger."
And suddenly there appeared with the angel a great multitude of the heavenly host, praising God and saying:
"Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!"
When the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to one another, "Let us go to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us."
So they hurried off and found Mary and Joseph and the Baby, who was lying in the manger.
After they had seen the Child, they spread the message they had received about Him.
And all who heard it were amazed at what the shepherds said to them.
But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
The shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen, which was just as the angel had told them.
When the eight days before His circumcision had passed, He was named Jesus, the name the angel had given Him before He was conceived.
And when the time of purification according to the Law of Moses was complete, His parents brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord
(as it is written in the Law of the Lord: "Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord"),
and to offer the sacrifice specified in the Law of the Lord: "A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons."
Now there was a man in Jerusalem named Simeon, who was righteous and devout. He was waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
The Holy Spirit had revealed to him that he would not see death before he had seen the Lord's Christ.
Led by the Spirit, he went into the temple courts. And when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for Him what was customary under the Law,
Simeon took Him in his arms and blessed God, saying:
"Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace.
For my eyes have seen Your salvation,
which You have prepared in the sight of all people,
a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel."
The Child's father and mother were amazed at what was spoken about Him.
Then Simeon blessed them and said to His mother Mary: "Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against,
so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed— and a sword will pierce your soul as well."
There was also a prophetess named Anna, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher, who was well along in years. She had been married for seven years,
and then was a widow to the age of eighty-four. She never left the temple, but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.
Coming forward at that moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.
When Jesus' parents had done everything required by the Law of the Lord, they returned to Galilee, to their own town of Nazareth.
And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.
Every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover.
And when He was twelve years old, they went up according to the custom of the Feast.
When those days were over and they were returning home, the boy Jesus remained behind in Jerusalem, but His parents were unaware He had stayed.
Assuming He was in their company, they traveled on for a day before they began to look for Him among their relatives and friends.
When they could not find Him, they returned to Jerusalem to search for Him.
Finally, after three days they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions.
And all who heard Him were astounded at His understanding and His answers.
When His parents saw Him, they were astonished. "Child, why have You done this to us?" His mother asked. "Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You."
"Why were you looking for Me?" He asked. "Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?"
But they did not understand the statement He was making to them.
Then He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them. But His mother treasured up all these things in her heart.
And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.

context.author: Traditionally Luke, a Gentile physician and traveling companion of the apostle Paul, who also wrote the book of Acts
context.genre: Historical narrative — Luke anchors the birth of Jesus in the wider history of the Roman world, then moves through a series of short scenes (shepherds, temple, boyhood) tied together by Mary's quiet reflection
context.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile Greek-speaking readership
context.setting: The chapter moves from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the town of David a few miles south of Jerusalem, where the shepherds keep their flocks in nearby fields. It then shifts to the temple courts in Jerusalem for the presentation and for the Passover visit when Jesus is twelve, before returning to Nazareth.
context.custom: Luke's word for "inn" (kataluma) can also mean a guest room, which is how the same word is used for the room of the Last Supper, so some readers picture a crowded family home rather than a roadside lodging. Newborns were wrapped in strips of cloth, and a manger was a feeding trough. A mother was ritually unclean for forty days after bearing a son (Leviticus 12), and the offering of two birds in place of a lamb was the provision for families who could not afford more. Pilgrims traveled to Passover in large family caravans, which explains how Joseph and Mary could go a full day before noticing Jesus was missing.
context.timelineImmediate: The chapter covers roughly twelve years in a series of snapshots: the birth and the shepherds, the naming at eight days, the presentation at about forty days, the quiet return to Nazareth, and then one scene from Jesus' boyhood at age twelve. It is the only passage in the Gospels that tells us anything about Jesus between infancy and adulthood.
context.timelineBible: Bethlehem as the birthplace fulfills Micah 5:2, and Simeon's phrase "a light for revelation to the Gentiles" draws on Isaiah 42:6 and 49:6. Luke's summary that Jesus "grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man" deliberately echoes the way 1 Samuel 2:26 describes the boy Samuel growing. Verse 2 has long been discussed by historians, and the BSB footnotes that it can also be read as "the census before Quirinius was governor of Syria."
context.sparkNotes: A decree from Caesar Augustus sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger. An angel announces the news to shepherds in the nearby fields, a heavenly host praises God, and the shepherds hurry to find the child and spread the word while Mary treasures it all in her heart. At the temple, the aged Simeon and the prophetess Anna recognize the infant Jesus, and Simeon warns Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul. The chapter closes with the twelve-year-old Jesus found in the temple among the teachers, saying He must be in His Father's house, and then returning to Nazareth in obedience.

translation.meaning: To bring good news. This is the verb behind our word "evangelize," and Luke's angel uses it of the news of Jesus' birth. The announcement is specifically described as "for all the people," not just for Israel.

occurrences.note: Luke uses this verb more than any other Gospel writer.

translation.meaning: A deliverer or rescuer. In Luke's world the word was also used of gods and emperors, so announcing a Savior born in a Bethlehem stable to shepherds is a pointed contrast with the grand titles of Caesar Augustus, whose decree opens the chapter.

Literally "throwing together" — turning events over and fitting the pieces together in her mind. The verb is used elsewhere for people conferring or debating, so Mary's pondering is an active, thoughtful weighing of what she has seen and heard.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's account of the birth of Jesus, told from Joseph's point of view.
Matthew's account of the return to Nazareth after the family's time in Egypt.

otBackground.note: The prophecy that the ruler of Israel would come from Bethlehem.
A servant given as a light to the nations — the background to Simeon's words in verse 32.
The law of purification after childbirth and the offering of two birds, followed in verses 22-24.
The consecration of every firstborn male to the Lord, quoted in verse 23.
The boy Samuel growing in favor with the Lord and with people, echoed in verse 52.

commentary.note: Henry observes that the shepherds were not shaken by the poverty they found: "The poverty and meanness in which they found Christ the Lord were no shock to their faith, who themselves knew what it was to live a life of comfortable communion with God in very poor and mean circumstances." He adds that just as the cross later became a stumbling-block to some, so the manger did, while others saw in it the wisdom and power of God.
commentary.blurb: Christ's humble birth didn't shake the shepherds' faith.

commentary.note: In The Everlasting Man, Chesterton notes that the Bethlehem cave was an ordinary stable used by the hill herdsmen. He reads the shepherds as the common people who had always been the makers of myths, and the Magi as the philosophers, so that both strands of the ancient world arrive at the same manger. His line: "The shepherds had found their Shepherd."
commentary.blurb: Simple shepherds and wise men both find the same child.

commentary.note: Preaching on verse 49, Spurgeon notes these are the first recorded words of Jesus and tells his hearers to "write that 'MUST' in capital letters." He hears surprise in the reply — Jesus is astonished they did not realize that God is His Father — and says of the boy that other things did not interest Him, but this thing absorbed Him.
commentary.blurb: Jesus' first words show He felt He must be in His Father's house.

commentary.note: Lewis does not comment on Luke 2, but in Miracles his chapter "The Grand Miracle" treats the birth in the manger as the center of Christian belief. He calls the Incarnation the miracle on which the others depend, and pictures a descent so deep that God goes down into the human world, and takes it back up with Him. That is how he understands "a Savior has been born to you." (Paraphrased; Lewis's works remain under copyright.)
commentary.blurb: The manger birth is the Grand Miracle: God becoming man.

overview.settingLine: Nazareth to Bethlehem, then the temple in Jerusalem.

history.t: Augustus rules the Mediterranean world, and Herod the Great governs Judea as Rome's client king.
Taxes and a census made foreign rule felt, keeping hopes for a Messiah alive.

customs.t: Luke's word can mean a guest room, so a crowded family home fits.
Poorer families offered two birds instead of a lamb.

overview.audience: Theophilus and a broad, largely Gentile readership
overview.author: Luke
overview.summary: A decree from Caesar Augustus sends Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger. Angels announce the news to shepherds, who hurry to find the child. Simeon and Anna recognize Him in the temple, and at twelve He is found in His Father's house.
overview.discussion: Mary "treasured" what she could not yet understand. Is faith more about understanding, or holding on?
overview.book: The third Gospel · 24 chapters. Written as an orderly account, with Acts as its sequel.
